source_text:
Anaphora Graeca
«Ἄξιον καὶ δίκαιόν ἐστιν ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, εὐχαριστεῖν σοι ἀδιαλείπτως ὑπὲρ πασῶν
τῶν εὐεργεσιῶν σου ὧν ἐδωρήσω ἡμῖν, πρῶτον μὲν ὅτι ἀπέστειλας ἡμῖν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ τὸν
ἅγιον παῖδά σου, τὸν σύνθρονον τῆς βασιλείας σου, τὸν συναΐδιόν σου υἱόν, τὸν Θεὸν
λόγον, ὃς 299 ἐλθὼν ἐπ' ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν, λαβὼν τὴν ἡμετέραν ἀνθρωπότητα ὁ
λόγος σὰρξ γενόμενος μὴ ὑπομείνας τροπήν, διὰ Πνεύματος ἁγίου σάρκα καὶ ψυχὴν
ἔννουν ἀνθρώπου ἔχων καὶ πάντα τὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας, οὐχ ὡς ἐν
ἀνθρώπῳ τινὶ ἐνοικήσας, ἀλλὰ αὐτὸς ὅλως ὁ Θεὸς λόγος τέλειος τελείως βρωθείς, οὐκ
ἀλλοιώσας τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα, οὐχὶ δύο ὑπάρχων, ἀλλ' εἷς βασιλεύς, εἷς Χριστός, εἷς
thought_title: Thanksgiving for the sending of the divine Word who became fully human
orientation: The anaphora opens with the congregation's prayer of thanksgiving addressed to God the Father for his benefits, especially the sending of his Son.
pass_a_gloss: It is worthy and just, our God, to give thanks to you unceasingly for all your benefits which you gave to us, first because you sent to us from heaven your holy servant, sharing your throne, your co-eternal Son, the divine Word, who coming in the last of the days, taking our humanity, the Word becoming flesh not undergoing change, through the Holy Spirit having flesh and a rational soul of a human and all the things of the human without sin, not as dwelling in some human, but he himself wholly the divine Word perfect perfectly made flesh, not altering the humanity, not being two, but one king, one Christ, one

choices.why: The glossary cast list gives παῖδά as a source form for Christ; servant preserves the literal sense of παῖς without importing 'Son' here, since υἱός appears separately in the same clause.

choices.english: the one sharing the throne of your kingdom
choices.why: The glossary English for σύνθρονον τῆς βασιλείας is 'sharing your throne'; expanding to 'the one sharing the throne of your kingdom' keeps the full genitive phrase literal.
The glossary English for Θεὸς λόγος is 'the divine Word'; the accusative form is rendered accordingly.
The glossary English for ἀνθρωπότητα is 'humanity'; the banned alternative 'human nature' is avoided.
The literal sense of βιβρώσκω is 'eaten'; this is the literal lane, so the odd eucharistic image is preserved rather than smoothed.
The literal sense of ἀλλοιόω is 'altering' or 'changing'; 'altering' keeps the force of the aorist participle without importing theological vocabulary.

pass_b_english: It is right and fitting, our God, to give you thanks unceasingly for all the benefits you have given us. First, because you sent us from heaven your holy Son, sharing your throne, your co-eternal Son, the divine Word. In these last days he came and took our humanity; the Word became flesh without undergoing change (John 1:14). Through the Holy Spirit he possessed human flesh and a rational soul, and everything that belongs to a human being, apart from sin. He did not dwell in some human being as a guest, but he himself, the divine Word, entirely perfect, was perfectly made flesh. He did not alter his humanity, and he is not two, but one king, one Christ, one.
notes: The numeral 299 appears in the source before ἐλθὼν; it is likely a page or section number from the edition and not part of the prayer text.

problems.quote: the one sharing the throne of your kingdom
problems.why: Glossary requires 'sharing your throne', not 'sharing the throne of your kingdom'.
βρωθείς is passive of βιβρώσκω, but context demands 'made flesh'/'incarnate', not 'eaten'.

edits.old: the one sharing the throne of your kingdom

problems.why: Glossary requires 'servant' for παῖς? No—brief maps παῖδά to Christ cast entry but doesn't fix English. However 'servant' is standard for παῖς in liturgical texts; brief's cast uses 'Son' forms. Check: glossary has no fixed term for παῖς, but 'servant' obscures Christological title.

βρωθείς means 'eaten/devoured,' not 'made flesh.' This is a scribal error or variant for σαρκωθείς? Source reads βρωθείς. But meaning is 'was perfectly eaten'? No—context demands incarnation. However as checker I must flag: English 'made flesh' doesn't match βρωθείς.
problems.fix: was perfectly made flesh [or eaten, if text is corrupt]

fixed: The English 'was perfectly made flesh' already matches the intended incarnational sense of the source, despite the textual variant βρωθείς; no change is needed.
The English 'your holy servant' was changed to 'your holy Son' to reflect the Christological title.

problems.quote: one king, one Christ, one Lord
problems.why: Source has three items (king, Christ, [one]), English supplies 'Lord' not in source.
problems.fix: one king, one Christ, one [something matching source's third term]
problems.ruling: Source ends 'εἷς βασιλεύς, εἷς Χριστός, εἷς' (one king, one Christ, one [implied]); English adds 'one Lord' not in source.

edits.old: one king, one Christ, one Lord.

fixed: The English supplied 'Lord' where the source has only 'one' as the third item; replaced with 'one' to match the source.

problems.quote: sharing your throne, your co-eternal Son, the divine Word
problems.why: Christ's titles vary unsystematically; 'one king' and 'one Lord' may seem like different figures.
problems.fix: Use consistent title or note equivalence.

edits.old: your holy Son, sharing your throne, your co-eternal Son, the divine Word.
edits.new: your holy Son, the one sharing your throne, your co-eternal Son, the divine Word.

fixed: The English already says 'one king, one Christ, one' which matches the source's 'one king, one Christ, one' and does not introduce a separate figure. The title variation is inherent in the source and the English preserves it.

dismissed.why: βρωθείς means 'eaten/devoured,' not 'made flesh'; nonsensical rendering.
dismissed.note: brotheis ("eaten") is a plain corruption of sarkotheis; "was perfectly made flesh" is the sensible reading.

dismissed.why: Missing 'Lord' (Κύριος) at end of source clause.
dismissed.note: The section source ends at "heis" because the chunk boundary splits "heis | Kyrios"; the English mirrors the cut. Fix the segmentation (or join across sections), not this translation.
